prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "ABBOTT LABORATORIES" (ticker ABT), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "ABT", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Abbott Laboratories
result.industry: Diversified healthcare: medical devices, diagnostics, nutrition and branded generic medicines
markets: Cardiac rhythm management, electrophysiology and heart failure devices
Core laboratory, rapid and molecular diagnostics
Cancer screening and precision oncology diagnostics (Exact Sciences: Cologuard, Oncotype DX)
Pediatric and adult nutrition (Similac, PediaSure, Ensure, Glucerna)
Branded generic pharmaceuticals in emerging markets

mission.statement: to help you live a healthier, fuller life.
mission.source: abbott.com, About Abbott page (2026): "At Abbott, we're driven by a shared mission: to help you live a healthier, fuller life."
mission.plain: Abbott wants its products to help people stay healthy and live longer, better lives.

about.plain: Abbott makes many kinds of health products. It sells small sensors that people with diabetes wear on their arm to check their blood sugar, and devices that fix heart rhythm and heart valve problems. It makes machines and tests that hospitals use to check blood and find diseases, including cancer screening tests. It also makes baby formula and nutrition drinks, and sells medicines in developing countries.
about.customers: Hospitals, labs, doctors, pharmacies, governments and everyday shoppers buying formula and nutrition drinks in more than 160 countries.
about.everyday: Similac baby formula, Ensure and PediaSure drinks, the FreeStyle Libre glucose sensor and the BinaxNOW COVID test are all Abbott products.

money.plain: glucose sensors, heart rhythm and heart valve devices, stents, pain-relief implants
lab blood-test machines and tests, rapid tests, and (from 2026) Cologuard cancer screening
baby formula (Similac) and adult drinks (Ensure, Glucerna)
branded generic medicines sold in emerging markets
Cologuard stool test, Oncotype DX and the Cancerguard multi-cancer blood test

money.part: Consumer biowearables (Lingo) and pulsed field ablation (Volt)
money.plain: over-the-counter glucose sensor for non-diabetics and new heart-ablation systems

result.summary: Abbott has a real but mixed competitive advantage: FreeStyle Libre is the world's largest CGM franchise ($7.6B of CGM sales in 2025) built on low-cost, high-volume sensor manufacturing, and its device and core-lab businesses enjoy regulatory barriers and installed-base switching costs. Nutrition and rapid diagnostics are more commoditised and have shrunk recently, and 2026 brought a serious Libre 3 sensor recall and heavier debt from the $23B Exact Sciences deal.

pricingPower.evidence: Devices and core-lab contracts hold price, but Abbott pays large rebates: rebates and chargebacks were $4.8B or 21.1% of gross sales subject to rebate in 2025, up from 17.4% in 2023 (FY2025 10-K); Libre has grown by lowering cost per sensor and widening reimbursement rather than raising price, and infant formula sales fell 1.2% in 2025 as volumes slipped.

moats.evidence: Similac, Ensure, PediaSure and FreeStyle Libre are household names, and the company holds thousands of device patents and FDA approvals, but hospital buyers choose devices more on clinical data and contract price than on the Abbott brand.

Core Laboratory analyzers (Alinity) are locked in with multi-year reagent contracts ($5.36B of 2025 Core Lab sales), and implanted pacemakers, defibrillators and neurostimulators keep patients on Abbott's platform; CGM users can switch more easily at the pharmacy.
LibreView data-sharing and app integrations with insulin pumps (e.g., Tandem, Insulet, Beta Bionics) create a modest ecosystem, but there is no strong user-to-user network effect.

Abbott makes CGM sensors in very high volumes, which let it price Libre below rivals and reach Diabetes Care sales of $7,998M in 2025 (+17.5%), and its $44.3B revenue base spreads sales, regulatory and R&D costs across 160+ countries.

US infant formula is a concentrated market with few FDA-approved plants (the 2022 Sturgis shutdown caused a national shortage), and cardiac rhythm management is effectively a three-player market with Medtronic and Boston Scientific.
Libre's low-price, mass-market approach once counter-positioned Dexcom's premium model, but Dexcom has since launched lower-cost and over-the-counter Stelo sensors.

High-volume, low-cost sensor and assay manufacturing is hard to copy, though the February 2026 Class I recall of Libre 3 / 3 Plus sensors (tied to one production line, 7 deaths and 860 serious injuries reported) shows the process is not flawless.

Exact Sciences' Cologuard is the leading US stool-based colorectal screening test with entrenched guideline status, but Abbott holds no single exclusive resource that rivals cannot eventually replicate.

customers.evidence: Libre has built a large, loyal user base with Diabetes Care growing 17.5% in 2025, and hospitals renew multi-year diagnostics contracts, but the 2022 formula recall and the 2026 Libre 3 sensor recall dented trust, and pediatric nutrition sales fell in 2025.

talent.evidence: Abbott employs about 115,000 people (10-K, end 2025) and is listed in Fortune's 2026 World's Most Admired Companies in medical products and equipment, though not among the top-50 All-Stars; it is a respected but not elite employer brand.

product.evidence: FreeStyle Libre is the world's best-selling CGM line, Abbott has leading positions in MitraClip/TriClip transcatheter valve repair, leadless pacing (AVEIR) and core-lab immunoassay (Alinity), and Cologuard leads stool-based colorectal screening; diagnostics and nutrition products are more commoditised.

threats: Libre 3 / 3 Plus Class I sensor recall (FDA, February 2026; 7 deaths and 860 serious injuries reported) could hurt trust and share versus Dexcom
Dexcom, Medtronic/MiniMed and new low-cost CGM entrants pressuring sensor prices, plus over-the-counter rivals to Lingo
Boston Scientific's Farapulse lead in pulsed field ablation and Watchman's lead over Amulet in left atrial appendage closure
Blood-based colorectal screening (Guardant Shield) and reimbursement changes threatening Cologuard
Integration risk and roughly $32.6B of debt after the $23B Exact Sciences acquisition
Infant formula litigation (NEC lawsuits) and continued pediatric nutrition volume declines
Post-COVID decline in rapid diagnostics (COVID testing sales fell from $1.6B in 2023 to $297M in 2025) and China volume-based procurement in diagnostics

ceo.name: Robert B. Ford
ceo.background: Bachelor's degree from Boston College, MBA from UC Berkeley Haas; joined Abbott in 1996 in diabetes care, ran the medical devices businesses and led the St. Jude Medical integration; chairman since December 2021

c1.evidence: Abbott leads continuous glucose monitoring, a fast-growing young market where its Diabetes Care sales rose 17.5% to $7,998M in 2025, but most of the company sits in mature diagnostics, nutrition and generics.

c2.evidence: Customers pick Libre for low cost and accuracy at scale and Alinity for its broad test menus, advantages that are durable but that Dexcom, Roche and others are actively contesting.

c3.evidence: Similac, Ensure and FreeStyle Libre are widely known and Libre is the volume leader in CGM, but Abbott is not the default leader across most of its fields the way Intuitive Surgical is in robotic surgery.

c4.evidence: Abbott's stated mission is "to help you live a healthier, fuller life" and it has pursued access-focused products like low-cost CGM, but its communications centre on financial targets as much as purpose.

c6.evidence: "reliable, diversified, baby formula" — the name mostly evokes a steady healthcare blue chip, an impression that is mostly positive though dented by the 2022 Sturgis formula recall and the 2026 Libre sensor recall.

c7.evidence: Its markets ride ageing populations and rising diabetes and heart disease; Abbott itself cites a $60B US cancer screening and precision oncology market for the Exact Sciences deal.

c8.evidence: Abbott has moved into consumer biowearables (Lingo), pulsed field ablation (Volt), and cancer diagnostics through the March 2026 Exact Sciences acquisition, including the Cancerguard multi-cancer blood test.

m1.evidence: Robert Ford has pushed Abbott toward biowearables and cancer diagnostics, but he is seen as a disciplined operator more than a visionary.

m2.evidence: Ford is a 30-year Abbott career executive (joined 1996) who has made long-term bets like Exact Sciences, but he is a hired professional CEO, not a founder.

m4.evidence: There is no clear public evidence either way on whether Ford's leadership style is servant leadership.

m5.evidence: Abbott keeps launching products (AVEIR, TriClip, Volt PFA, Libre 3 Plus, Lingo) on an R&D budget of $2,942M in 2025, but this is an inherited engineering culture rather than one Ford built.

m6.evidence: Ford came up through Abbott's diabetes and medical device businesses, but his education is in business (Boston College, Berkeley Haas MBA), not engineering.

m7.evidence: Ford redirected Abbott to mass COVID-19 testing in 2020 (BinaxNOW, ID NOW), a real public-health contribution, but there is little else to set him apart on character.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Robert Ford at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar university was found.

m8b.evidence: Ford keeps a low public profile and is not known for a distinctive personality.

m9.evidence: Under Ford, sales rose from $34,608M (2020) to $44,328M (2025) and the 2025 operating margin was 18.2%, but adjusted EPS of $5.15 in 2025 was still below 2022's $5.34, and the stock fell about 19% over the 52 weeks to October 2026.

m10.evidence: Abbott is not known for frugality; SG&A was $12,332M or 27.8% of sales in 2025.

c10.evidence: Abbott sells in more than 160 countries, and products such as Libre sensors, heart devices, blood tests, infant formula and affordable generic medicines reach hundreds of millions of people.

p2.evidence: Implantable heart devices, accurate high-volume biosensors and cancer screening are hard and important, while formula and generic drugs are easier to copy.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose in 4 of the last 5 years ($34,608M in 2020, $43,075M, $43,653M, then $40,109M in 2023, $41,950M and $44,328M in 2025); it fell in 2023 as COVID testing faded.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from 15.5% (2020) to 18.2% (2025) but is below 2021's 19.6%, and gross margin before amortization was roughly flat (56.6% in 2020 vs 56.4% in 2025).

f3.evidence: Equity is positive at $51,762M, but after the Exact Sciences deal debt was $32,608M against $5,603M of cash and short-term investments at June 30, 2026, about 4.4 times 2025 free cash flow of $7,395M.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $5,357M (2020) to $8,053M (2025) and operating cash flow from $7,901M to $9,566M, but both are below their 2021 peaks of $8,425M and $10,533M.

v1.evidence: FreeStyle Libre is the cheapest widely reimbursed CGM with long wear time, a clear reason to choose it, but Dexcom is often preferred for pump integration and many Abbott businesses have no clear best-in-class edge.

v2.evidence: Abbott is listed in Fortune's 2026 World's Most Admired Companies in medical products and equipment but is not one of the top-50 All-Stars.

c5.evidence: Millions of people with diabetes rely on Libre sensors, heart patients on Abbott pacemakers and valve repair devices, hospitals on its lab tests, and parents on Similac, so many people would notice right away if it disappeared.
